dct_description_sm: This dataset contains the supplementary materials of the study: "Caring and killing: exploring human-animal relationships and moral distress in cattle veterinary practice". Abstract: Within cattle veterinary practice, the subjects of care constitute both sentient beings and individual commodity units that are usually destined for eventual slaughter. This paradox presents potential challenges, with decisions involving financial constraints being one of the most common causes of moral distress among veterinarians. We conducted semi-structured interviews with cattle veterinarians, seeking to understand how participants construct and navigate their relationship with the animals they care for, and whether and how they experience and cope with ethical challenges and moral distress arising from their work. Interviews (n = 21) were recorded, transcribed, and underwent reflexive thematic analysis. Analysis resulted in three major themes, each with underlying subthemes: 1) The professional box: navigating the caring-killing paradox within the structural confines of the profession; 2) ‘They’re dealing with more than you think’: animal perspective-taking as an embodied, relational practice; and 3) The fall-out: moral conflict, rationalization, and ameliorating the costs of persistence. Our results describe how nested levels of context shape cattle veterinarians’ professional experiences. Further, moral distress related to individual farm-level scenarios may be structurally produced and locked into place by both economic and social forces. To promote sustainable veterinary careers and improve animal welfare outcomes, we emphasize the need to better equip veterinary team members with the knowledge and skills to navigate ethical challenges in cattle practice.
